The foundational concept of first-order drives establishes a dualism between physiological quiescence and aversive disturbance. These are not merely descriptive but structurally encoded as binary manifolds within a dynamical system framework. Each drive initiates through a physiological excitement that propels the organism toward a terminal state—either satiation or avoidance. This duality implies a symmetry in the underlying mechanism: the same initiating cause can lead to opposite outcomes depending on the organism's internal state. In GSI, this manifests as a Bayesian update where the likelihood of quiescence or aversion is conditioned on arousal signals. In GSE, it translates into a state transition graph where each node corresponds to a drive state and edges represent action policies. The failure mode occurs when the system cannot distinguish between competing drives, leading to bifurcation or oscillation around unstable equilibria. The mathematical structure supports recursive nesting of drives, enabling hierarchical planning and adaptive control.
